beats.headline: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
beats.subline: The answer is always the same, but the behavior changes based on what you pass.
beats.narration: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference? New developers get tripped up here constantly. If you reassign an object inside a method, it fails, but if you mutate it, it succeeds. Let's clear this up.

beats.title: The Reference Variable
beats.subtitle: Stacks, Heaps, and Copies

nodes.label: Method Call
nodes.detail: Copies the address, not the object

beats.narration: Think of the heap object as a house and the variable as a piece of paper with its address. When you pass a variable, Java photocopies the paper. Both papers point to the same house.

beats.title: Mutation vs. Reassignment

steps.explanation: Follows the copied address to the heap. The caller sees the change.
Changes the local address on the paper. The caller's paper remains unchanged.

beats.narration: If you mutate the object, you are following the copied address to the heap. If you reassign the parameter, you are just writing a new address on your local photocopy. The caller never sees the swap.

beats.title: Primitive vs Reference

top.label: Primitive (int, boolean)
top.code:
int a = 10;
int b = a; // b is a copy of 10

bottom.label: Reference Type (Objects)
bottom.code:
Car a = new Car();
Car b = a; // b is a copy of the address

beats.narration: Primitives copy the raw data. Objects copy the address. This aliasing is why two variables can point to the same object. It is a feature, until you accidentally corrupt shared state.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Objects are copied by reference address
Reassignment is local to the method
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Why Object.clone() is a trap →
beats.narration: You now understand the stack-heap split. In Part 2, we look at why Object dot clone is a legacy minefield and how to build proper copies.

beats.headline: Stop using Object.clone() in your production code.
beats.subline: It bypasses constructors and creates shallow copies that lead to silent bugs.
beats.narration: Stop using Object dot clone. It was a mistake in Java 1.0. It performs a shallow copy, bypasses your constructors, and requires a marker interface that does nothing.

beats.title: Shallow vs. Deep Copy
beats.subtitle: The nested object problem
beats.narration: Shallow copies just copy the reference to nested objects. If you modify the nested object in the copy, you mutate the original. A deep copy recursively creates new instances for everything.

beats.title: The Cloneable Failure

steps.explanation: Native JVM call. Bypasses your constructors entirely.
Forces ugly try-catch blocks for a method that shouldn't fail.

beats.narration: Super dot clone is a native call that ignores your constructors. It skips invariant checks and forces you to deal with checked exceptions. It is fragile, dangerous, and outdated.

beats.title: The Shallow Copy Gotcha
beats.caption: Mutating the copy affects the original
beats.narration: Because clone is shallow, e2 shares the same address object as e1. Changing the city in the clone silently corrupts the original instance. This is why we use copy constructors instead.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Copy constructors vs. Static Factories →
beats.narration: Cloneable is a dead end. In Part 3, we implement proper copy constructors and static factory methods that handle deep copies cleanly.

beats.headline: Copy constructors are the gold standard.
beats.subline: They are explicit, type-safe, and work perfectly with final fields.
beats.narration: Copy constructors are the gold standard. They are explicit, type-safe, and work perfectly with final fields. They make it obvious when you are creating a deep copy versus a shallow one.

beats.title: Implementing a Copy Constructor

steps.explanation: String is immutable, so sharing the reference is safe.
Explicitly create new instances for mutable fields.

beats.narration: For immutable fields like Strings, just copy the reference. For mutable fields like Address or List, call their own copy constructors or create a new wrapper. This is explicit and safe.

beats.title: Clone vs. Copy Constructor
beats.narration: Copy constructors win on every metric. They run your validation logic, require no casting, and make deep copying a deliberate design choice rather than an accidental side effect.

beats.title: Static Factory Alternative

steps.explanation: Clean, readable API for copying objects.

beats.narration: You can also use a static copy factory. It is just a wrapper around the copy constructor, but it provides a more fluent API and can even return cached instances if needed.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Defensive Copying & TOCTOU bugs →
beats.narration: Copy constructors are your best friend. In Part 4, we finish with defensive copying to protect your internal state from external mutation.

beats.headline: Your private fields are not actually private.
beats.subline: If you return mutable references, callers can destroy your internal invariants.
beats.narration: Your private fields are not actually private. If you return a mutable reference from a getter, the caller can modify your internal state. Defensive copying is the only way to lock it down.

beats.title: The Defensive Copy Pattern

steps.explanation: Copy before validation to avoid TOCTOU race conditions.
Check the private copy, not the caller's reference.

beats.narration: Always copy before validating. If you validate first, a concurrent thread could mutate the date in the gap between the check and the copy. This is a classic TOCTOU race condition.

beats.title: The Getter Leak
beats.caption: Don't return the original reference!

lines.text: return new Date(start.getTime()); // Return a copy!
// If you return 'start', the caller can:

beats.narration: Never return the raw reference in a getter. Always return a defensive copy. If you return the original, the caller can call setTime on it and bypass your class invariants entirely.

beats.title: Modern Alternatives
beats.narration: The best way to avoid defensive copying is to use immutable types. Java 8's java dot time package makes defensive copying obsolete. Use Instant or LocalDate and stop worrying about aliasing.
